extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, federal judges, legislators, and administrative law practitioners interested in separation-of-powers and administrative adjudication reform
extracted.subtask_description: Drafting and evaluating a statutory reform that requires report-and-recommendation procedures and Article III de novo review for agency adjudications that determine private rights, and that limits judicial deference to agency statutory interpretations in criminal or hybrid cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report-and-recommendation requirement for private-rights adjudications
rubrics_metrics.description: After a hearing required by section 554 of the Administrative Procedure Act, the agency, officer thereof, or administrative law judge presiding pursuant to section 556(b), shall submit proposed findings of fact and recommendations for the disposition, by a judge of a federal court having jurisdiction, for any matter which may determine the private rights of any party to the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion prescribes that agency adjudicators do not enter final orders when private rights are at stake but instead produce proposed findings and recommendations for an Article III judge to decide. The proposed statutory text borrows the mechanism used in bankruptcy and magistrate contexts. It covers adjudications after an APA §554 hearing and those presided over by ALJs under §556(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections timeline and de novo judicial review procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Within fourteen days after being served with a copy, any party may serve and file written objections to such proposed findings and recommendations as provided by rules of court. A judge of the court shall make a de novo determination of those portions of the report or specified proposed findings or recommendations to which objection is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies a 14-day objection window and requires the district judge to review de novo the portions objected to; the judge may accept, reject, or modify findings/recommendations in whole or in part, receive further evidence, or recommit the matter to the agency with instructions. Use of familiar magistrate/bankruptcy procedures provides concrete procedural steps and sample judicial authorities (accept/reject/modify; receive evidence; recommit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent-of-parties exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon the consent of the parties, pursuant to their specific written requests, the agency may forgo these procedures and enter final orders it otherwise has authority to enter by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows parties to waive the report-and-recommendation procedures by specific written consent, enabling agencies to enter final orders when all parties agree. This is an explicit exception limiting the rule when parties voluntarily opt into agency finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: applies to adjudications of private rights (including independent agencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedures of section 1 shall apply to any adjudication of private rights conducted by any independent agency, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in existing governing statutes. Private rights include those that would be determined by traditional actions at common law, and include the right to be free of deprivation of property by fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the covered universe: (1) any adjudication that determines 'private rights,' (2) coverage explicitly extends to independent agencies even if existing statutes suggest otherwise, and (3) gives an explicit definition/example of private rights (traditional common law claims; right to be free of deprivation of property by fine). This guidance helps classify which agency matters trigger the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: When agencies certify the entire record to the agency for decision, their final decision must be a report-and-recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency that does not preside over the hearing requires the entire record to be certified to it for decision, as permitted by section 557(b), the agency may follow the procedures of that section, except that its final decision must also be a report of proposed findings of fact and recommendations for the disposition of a judge of a federal court having jurisdiction over such matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents agencies from sidestepping the report-and-recommendation requirement by using §557(b) certification; even when the agency receives the certified record, its 'final decision' must be cast as a report and recommendation to an Article III judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: De novo review required when life or liberty at stake
rubrics_metrics.description: If life or liberty is at stake, review of both the law and the facts must be de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative and doctrinal rule: core private rights implicating life or liberty cannot be determined finally by agencies without Article III de novo review of both legal and factual determinations. This serves as a bright-line protection for the most fundamental rights (cited in the text as uncontested under modern doctrine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional private rights require Article III adjudication and de novo review
rubrics_metrics.description: When traditional private rights are at stake, Article III adjudication is necessary—meaning that all findings of fact and law must be reviewed de novo by an Article III court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms that 'traditional' private-rights claims (those that would have received protection at common law) warrant full Article III treatment, not mere agency finality or limited review. The text contrasts this with newer 'entitlement' or 'new property' claims that might receive lesser protection (appellate review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish private rights, public rights, and privileges (entitlements/new property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Private rights are the traditional Lockean rights to life and personal security, liberty, and private property. Public rights belong to the public as a whole and need not receive judicial review of how government handles them. Privileges like welfare benefits are 'entitlements' conveyed by government largesse and may be treated differently; 'new property' (e.g., social security benefits, government employment) can exist at government's grace and need not always receive the same protection as traditional property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the classificatory rubric for which adjudications require Article III protections: identify whether the claimed interest is a private right (core/common-law), a public right, or a governmental 'privilege'/entitlement. The article notes policy and doctrinal tradeoffs (e.g., courts would be overwhelmed if all new property claims required full Article III adjudication) and suggests appellate review can protect many entitlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute must address Chevron/deference for hybrid criminal-administrative statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: In the cases governed by this Act, and in any criminal case, the federal courts shall defer to agency interpretations of their governing statutes only to the extent the courts believe such interpretations are correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires a statutory solution to the Chevron problem in hybrid criminal-administrative contexts (and more broadly for cases covered by the Act): courts should give no deference beyond the degree they consider correct (effectively rejects or severely limits Chevron deference in these contexts). The paper notes that Congress could declare that lower courts should not defer to agency interpretations that lead to criminal penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three required components of the reform statute
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple statute could ensure this same review in the administrative context. It would need to do just three things: provide for the report and recommendation structure, define the adjudications at stake, and provide a solution to the problem of Chevron deference in hybrid criminal-administrative statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-level drafting checklist for reformers: (1) create the report-and-recommendation mechanism; (2) precisely define which adjudications (i.e., private-rights matters) trigger the mechanism; (3) specify how courts should treat agency statutory interpretations (particularly in criminal/hybrid cases). This functions as a minimal specification for any legislative text implementing the article's proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bankruptcy and magistrate systems as procedural precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: There is already precedent for the kind of review proposed above. Congress can borrow from the existing bankruptcy statute and the statute governing magistrate judges, which require bankruptcy courts and magistrate judges, respectively, to prepare reports and recommendations for de novo Article III review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical drafting guidance: adopt proven legislative language and procedural rules from 28 U.S.C. §157 (bankruptcy) and §636 (magistrates) (including objection timing, de novo standard, remand/recommit options) to design workable procedures that courts and agencies already understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional authority to limit deference in criminal contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress can in the meantime declare that lower federal courts should not defer to those interpretations [of agencies] [that lead to criminal penalties].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms that statutory reform (rather than waiting for Supreme Court intervention) can change judicial deference doctrine in contexts where agency interpretations create criminal liability. This is an actionable legislative option and a policy recommendation to protect Article III rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of administrative acts by function (rulemaking = legislative; enforcement = executive; adjudicating private rights = judicial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining primary rules of conduct through rulemaking, enforcing those rules, and adjudicating private rights correspond to legislative, executive, and judicial functions, respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal rubric for sorting administrative actions into separation-of-powers categories. The article argues that dissolving administrative-law fictions allows better classification and that some administrative acts clearly align with one branch and should be allocated accordingly (with corresponding procedural safeguards).
